rationale: The Latin anchor *obscurari* (to be darkened/obscured) could point to either sense, but the Old English lemma *a-þiéstrian* is built on *þéostre* (darkness) and carries a primary sense of becoming dark or overcast. The gloss "overcloud" and the attestation in a chronicle context (likely describing an eclipse or darkening of the sky) favor the literal, meteorological sense of overcloud.v.01 (become covered with clouds / become dark). The abstract sense obscure.v.03 is less likely given the concrete physical darkness implied by the root.
